analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before the government searches Americans' communications or buys their personal data.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees; no committee or floor action has followed.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite parts of the foreign surveillance law so that government agencies cannot search the contents of Americans' phone and internet communications collected under Section 702 without a warrant or a narrow emergency, consent, or cybersecurity exception. It would also make it illegal for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to buy Americans' location records, communication contents, and other personal data from data brokers instead of getting a court order. It would relieve small businesses and building custodians from being forced to help the government intercept communications, and it would give civil-liberties lawyers a bigger role in the secret surveillance court. The trade-off: it extends the underlying bulk-surveillance authority until April 2028.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday Americans who use phones, email, and the internet. Today, agencies can search databases of collected communications for an American's messages without a warrant, and police and intelligence agencies can buy location and communication records from data brokers that no court ever reviewed. The bill would end both practices except under narrow exceptions, and would add privacy advocates to the secret court that approves surveillance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who uses a phone or internet

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any government employee from running a warrantless search for the contents of an American's communications collected under Section 702, with exceptions only for a court warrant, a life-or-death emergency, consent, or limited defensive cybersecurity searches.

Makes it illegal for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to buy Americans' communication records, location information, or illegitimately obtained data from a third party like a data broker in exchange for anything of value, and bars evidence obtained that way from being used in court.
Requires agencies to get a real court order, under the strictest applicable legal standard, before compelling a third party to hand over an American's records.

Ends the ability to compel building custodians and other non-provider businesses to assist government surveillance by sunsetting the expanded 'electronic communication service provider' definition on December 31, 2026.

Expands the role of privacy and civil-liberties experts in the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, gives them access to unredacted court records, and lets them petition for review up to the Supreme Court.

Requires the Director of National Intelligence to declassify, to the extent possible, the type of services at issue in secret FISA court opinions, and requires quarterly public reports on directives issued to service providers.

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence and law enforcement agencies would lose warrantless access to Americans' communications and would have to obtain court orders instead of purchasing data. Data brokers would lose government agencies as customers for Americans' personal records. Telecommunications and internet companies would get relief from compelled assistance but face more limited legal immunity when they help the government.

drawbacks.text: The bill extends the underlying Section 702 bulk-surveillance authority until April 20, 2028, keeping the program itself in place longer than it otherwise would expire.

The warrantless-search ban contains exceptions — emergency, consent, and cybersecurity — and information from emergency queries that are later denied is barred from proceedings, but the annual compliance check is reported to Congress, not the public.

The data-broker ban only covers records obtained 'in exchange for anything of value' and only certain record types, so data acquired without payment or outside the defined categories may remain obtainable.
The limits on directives to certain service providers and the sunset of the expanded provider definition take effect December 31, 2026, so the new protections lapse unless Congress renews them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are substantial and direct: a warrant requirement for searches of Americans' communications and a ban on buying personal data to dodge the Constitution. The main cost is embedded in the bill itself — the extension of the bulk-collection authority to 2028 — which reformers accepted as the price of attaching these restrictions. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how strictly the exceptions are policed, and the bill's own oversight of those exceptions runs only to Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees in March 2026, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced H.R. 7816 on March 5, 2026, joined by Reps. Crane and Clyde, and seven Republicans total are listed as cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence; the action history shows no markup, hearing, vote, or other action since the referral.

The bill text contains a warrant requirement for Section 702 queries of Americans' communications, the data-broker purchase ban titled the 'Fourth Amendment Is Not For Sale Act,' and an extension of FISA Title VII authorities to April 20, 2028.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, intelligence agencies and data brokers keep the current arrangement: warrantless searches of Americans' collected communications and the ability to buy personal data without a court order.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and data brokers, so far

against.role: Opponents of warrant requirements for Section 702 searches
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed warrant requirements for Section 702 queries of Americans during the 2024 reauthorization debate, when a similar House amendment failed by a single vote; the intelligence committees that oversee these programs have not advanced this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All eight listed supporters are Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors; however, warrant requirements for FISA searches have historically drawn bipartisan support and bipartisan opposition in the House.

industries.note: Data brokers make money collecting and reselling Americans' location data, communication records, and device data; agencies buy it because no warrant is needed. The ban would end that government revenue stream, which exists precisely because it lets the state bypass the Fourth Amendment.

The FBI, NSA, and other agencies would lose the ability to search Americans' collected communications without a warrant and to purchase personal data from brokers; every restriction in the bill narrows their access to information about United States persons.

industries.industry: Telecommunications, internet, and cloud service providers
industries.note: Providers would gain court review of surveillance directives and relief from compelled assistance after the expanded provider definition sunsets, but Section 207 narrows their civil immunity when they assist the government without a court order, adding legal risk. Their interest in fewer compelled surveillance obligations runs alongside their customers' privacy interests.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in two committees — including the Intelligence committee that oversees the programs it would restrict — since its March 2026 referral, with a small all-Republican cosponsor list and roughly ten months left in the Congress. In the 2024 reauthorization fight, a similar warrant requirement failed on the House floor by one vote despite broad support, and this bill has not reached even a committee vote. The most likely outcome is that it dies without a vote when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
